c1694d54ef326451: When it comes to cyberattacks that shut down power grids, drinking-water systems, and other critical infrastructure, AI doesn’t – yet – turn script kiddies into sophisticated, nation-state attackers. But “the potential is there,” according to operational technology (OT) security experts.

"One thing that we've relied on for years is security by obscurity when it comes to utilities," said Steve Swick, former chief information security officer at American Electric Power. "The knowledge needed to do some of that stuff is getting less likely to be necessary," Swick added during a media panel ahead of the publication of Frenos' State of AI in Security report.
AI makes it easier and faster for human attackers to target critical infrastructure, gain access to utilities and manufacturing plants, and perform OT system reconnaissance.

“Basic access can recon documentation, and distill through that documentation very quickly to find out critical design features of your plant and facility,” said Paul Shaver, head of OT at Armadin, during the panel. “I can download the manual for almost any automation controller, parse through that very quickly, and come up with ways that I can exploit a dedicated feature of something that was not secure by design.”

Armadin is Kevin Mandia’s new security startup that uses swarms of autonomous AI agents to simulate real-world cyberattacks. Prior to joining Armadin, Shaver spent six years as the global OT practice leader at Mandia’s earlier company, Mandiant, which Google acquired in 2022.

“I will fly my Mandiant flag for a second and try to steer away from the fear, uncertainty, and death of the world is coming to an end, and every script kiddie is now a very sophisticated nation-state adversary. But I’m not going to say the potential is not there, because the tools are improving such that the access to information is so much quicker.”

At Armadin, and with an AI assist, “I'm very quickly building tools in days that would normally have taken me months,” Shaver said. “If it can do that for me, it's doing something similar for the folks that have a very basic skill set. I wouldn't go so far as to script kiddies yet, but as the models improve, that becomes more of a possibility in this space.”

Plus, as AI lowers the technical barriers to would-be OT hackers, “it advances the timeline,” said Harry Thomas, chief technology officer and co-founder of Frenos, a security company that does AI pentesting for OT environments.

“If a better-than-average script kiddie can now perform attacks,” Thomas said, “You have more threat actors out there. There's an acceleration in timeline, more attacks could be happening, and from a defensive position, you might not know who your threat actor is anymore.”
Testing the power of LLMs to help plan attacks

The Frenos report, published Wednesday, examined the extent to which AI could help someone plan an attack on industrial systems. To do this, it ran several AI models through 16,980 tests between October 2025 and September 2026. These included 13,884 decision attempts, 2,520 planning attempts, and 576 simulated attacks.

The company won’t disclose the models or providers’ names, but said it tested six frontier models, two US open weight models, and two foreign open weight models, on three kinds of tasks: choosing one action, planning the steps to a goal, and working through a simulated scenario.

Each test gave the model background information and a set of attack actions to choose from. Before choosing, each model received details about assets, networks, and known weaknesses, plus the access each action required.
Frenos then checked whether the model’s choice matched the required outcome. Depending on the model, between 6 percent and 47 percent of the choices passed.

These tests found that the strongest three frontier models succeeded in about 90 percent of their planning attempts – meaning they produced a workable attack plan – but these same models weren’t consistent: 60 percent, 62.9 percent, and 74.3 percent of the attack plans passed every repeat.

“A plan can look sensible and still leave out something essential,” according to the report. “The models had information about the task, but some answers skipped a step or assumed access that the plan had not established.”

Meanwhile, the most successful of the four open weight models – a non-US model – achieved a 36.2 percent overall success rate. That figure, however, was still higher than the overall success rates of three other US frontier models, which scored 31.9 percent, 18.8 percent, and 17.9 percent, respectively.

“We're seeing that even though AI models help us accelerate our tooling, accelerate our access and knowledge transfer, they are still prone to hallucinations – aka mistakes,” Thomas said. “We still think human judgment remains essential for these AI models to make the threat actors achieve whatever mission or goal they're trying to achieve.”

In these tests, no humans asked the models to correct their plans, whereas in a real-life attack, a miscreant who understood the target could spot a gap in the AI’s plan, provide more information, and ask the model to revise its answer.

“On top of that, when we were testing the AI models, we used a harness that was pretty simple: Here's some information. Here's the context. Give me an answer,” Thomas said. “A more capable harness could have given these AI models more of an edge.”

Based on the findings, Frenos recommends actions for OT defenders to take, starting with a layered defense. This involves segmenting networks, limiting remote access and user permissions, and testing recovery steps.
“We have our business continuity plans and disaster recovery plans for a reason,” Thomas said. “Let's execute them.” ®

It has plummeted more than 40 per cent since the start of the year, placing it among the world’s worst-performing indexes.
The MSCI has cited investor concerns over “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures” as well as coordinated trading behaviour that has affected price information.
It is considering reclassifying Indonesia as a “standalone market”, which could force investment funds tracking the MSCI’s emerging market indexes to sell Indonesian holdings.
On Monday, Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) boss Jeffrey Hendrik announced measures to improve market transparency, including publicly providing more information on small shareholders.
The IDX would also remove “all shares with high shareholding concentration from the composite stock price index” to provide a more reasonable picture of JCI movements.
Indonesia’s economy has been hit hard by surging fuel prices due to the Middle East war.
The country of 287 million people is a net oil importer, but the government has insisted on leaving heavily subsidised fuel prices unchanged, despite struggling with high costs.
As food and commodities prices have risen, albeit within the target range, the economic strain has triggered protests, and Prabowo’s ratings are at a record low.
Today he said the country faced “many” difficulties and disruptions.
“We are not afraid. We have strength, we have courage, and we are willing to make sacrifices,” Prabowo said.
“We do not know the meaning of surrender... If necessary, we will carry out massive savings. We will be even more thrifty later on.”
Indonesia’s central bank today kept its key lending rate steady at 5.75 per cent after three hikes so far this year. — AFP
a9b74b59016f0a72: BERLIN, Oct 21 — Sebastian Vettel has revealed that his first contact with Ferrari came after his second Formula One world title, but he turned the Scuderia down at the time because he was happy and successful at Red Bull, reported German Press Agency (dpa).
“The first contact came in 2012 after the second title,” Vettel said in a documentary about him by public broadcaster ARD, titled Being Sebastian Vettel.
Vettel said he received a letter from then Ferrari president Luca di Montezemolo congratulating him, “without referring to anything else”.
But Ferrari, looking to return to the winning ways it had enjoyed a few years earlier during the Michael Schumacher era, went a step further.
Vettel said he had “a very secret meeting” with Di Montezemolo, during which “he asked, what is the contractual situation, do you want to drive for Ferrari?”
Vettel said he saw no reason to move at the time.
“So I turned them down, but of course I left the door open a little bit,” he said.
Vettel won two more world titles with Red Bull in 2012 and 2013, but eventually joined Ferrari in 2015 after a winless final season with the team.
He won 14 races for the Scuderia out of 53 victories in his Formula One career, but failed to secure a world title with Ferrari.

Aston Martin’s German driver Sebastian Vettel attends a presser ahead of the Abu Dhabi Formula One Grand Prix at the Yas Marina Circuit in the Emirati city of Abu Dhabi November 17, 2022. — AFP pic
He left the team after the 2020 season and retired in 2022 following two seasons with Aston Martin.
The four-part documentary, available from tomorrow, also explores the sacrifices his parents made to finance his racing career in its early days.

“Of course I was aware that the financial situation was tense, that it wasn’t easy when the next reminder notice arrived at home,” Vettel said, adding that he had felt a responsibility to deliver from his early karting days onwards.
Vettel became the youngest world champion at the age of 23 in 2010.
However, he is set to lose that record to Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who is 20 and has his first chance to clinch the 2026 title on Sunday at the United States (US) Grand Prix.
Others appearing in the documentary include Vettel’s former Red Bull mentor Helmut Marko and Lewis Hamilton, his long-time rival who became a friend.
Like Vettel, Hamilton has interests beyond motorsport.
Vettel also discusses former German economy minister Robert Habeck of the Green Party, reflecting his engagement with environmental protection and sustainability.
The documentary opens with Vettel holding a non-F1 trophy — a glass rhinoceros he received after being named Environmentalist of the Year in early 2026.
“I believe that the path I have now begun to follow is sustainable in the sense that it brings me fulfilment,” Vettel said. — Bernama-dpa
890c471910518c1f: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 21 — Malaysian consumers’ empowerment level has improved from moderate to high, with the 2025 Consumer Empowerment Index (CEI) recording an overall score of 70.36 per cent, up from 63.1 per cent in 2020.

Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali said the increase of 7.26 percentage points reflected consumers’ growing knowledge, confidence and ability to make informed decisions and take action to protect their rights.
“The increase in the score is not merely a statistical figure, but a true reflection of changes in the attitudes and actions of Malaysians as consumers,” he said in a statement today.

He said the Redress Action domain recorded the largest improvement, rising by 10.74 percentage points to 66.84 per cent, indicating that consumers were becoming more capable of lodging complaints and seeking redress when their rights were infringed.
The Purchase Decision domain improved by 7.11 percentage points to 75.91 per cent, while the Financial Literacy domain rose by 3.97 percentage points to 66.47 per cent.
Armizan said the CEI study assessed consumer empowerment across three key areas: financial literacy, purchase decisions, and understanding and exercising the right to seek redress and compensation.

He said the study was first conducted in 2020 to establish a baseline, with the 2025 CEI serving as a follow-up assessment. Benchmarking against the European Union and South Korea was also undertaken to ensure the study’s standards and quality.

Separately, Armizan said the Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry (KPDN) would continue to strengthen the Student Consumer Movement (GPS) as a platform for consumer education and advocacy among students at higher education institutions (IPT).
He said 196 GPS clubs had been registered nationwide, with students helping to raise awareness of consumer rights and responsibilities while promoting smart, ethical and responsible consumption.

The 2026 National Student Consumer Movement Assembly, held at the Universiti Pertahanan Nasional Malaysia (UPNM) from Oct 19 to 21, brought together 200 participants from 100 higher education institutions.

Activities included the GPS Exploration Challenge 2026, field visits with KPDN Kuala Lumpur enforcement officers, knowledge-sharing sessions, GPS Idea Lab presentations and the presentation of Food Bank Assistance Grants (i-FB). — Bernama
ff5f836c6900ec9b: WASHINGTON, Oct 21 — Stephen Hubbard, an American taken captive by Russian forces years ago in Ukraine, has been freed and was “on his way back home”, US President Donald Trump said today.
Russian President Vladimir Putin first announced the prisoner release during a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Russian news agencies reported.
Putin reportedly said that Hubbard was at Pulkovo Airport in Saint Petersburg, adding that Witkoff had thanked the Russian leader for the release.
Hubbard, a retired English teacher in his 70s, was sentenced in a closed trial in October 2024 to nearly seven years in prison for “mercenary work” on behalf of Ukraine, a charge he denies.
Trump said that Hubbard’s release was secured without need for a “swap” with Moscow.
“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” the American president wrote on his Truth Social platform.
“The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
However, Trump also tied Hubbard’s release to the recent suspension of some American sanctions and tariffs on Moscow.
“If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt,” he wrote in another Truth Social post.
Today’s announcement came as Witkoff met to brief Putin on his meeting with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo a day earlier, which the American envoy described as “productive”.
Trump had said on Tuesday that he had asked Putin for Hubbard’s release.
“I’ve been talking to him at length. I’ve asked him to release him. Let’s see what happens,” Trump told journalists in Washington.
Today, Witkoff said Trump and “our whole nation sends their thanks because of Stephen Hubbard,” calling Putin a “humanitarian”. — AFP
485af63f3c362602: Nvidia has proposed a new way to keep corporate AI agents in line.

Nvidia on Wednesday introduced its OpenShell Reference Architecture. Based on the company's OpenShell secure runtime, It's a recipe for creating, operating, observing, and policing AI agents using OpenShell on Nvidia hardware.

"Nvidia created OpenShell to give agents the freedom to do useful work within clearly defined boundaries — contained, monitored and under control," CEO Jensen Huang said in a canned statement. "With the OpenShell Reference Architecture, agents can think on Rubin, act on Vera and be governed on BlueField."

AI agents are touted as a powerful automation technology. The reality is that they can be unruly, as demonstrated by security testing OpenAI and Anthropic conducted, during which their models exceeded their remit and attacked third-party organizations.

Developers of existing agents, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, and OpenCode, therefore include controls that limit access to tools like curl and bash.Devs also create sandboxes to isolate an agentic process from the host, so that if agents go awry they're contained.
OpenShell sits a level above that with a runtime that extends sandboxing to govern gateway-brokered credentials, identity and policy boundaries, and (eventually) routing and workflows too.
At least mostly – OpenShell still has a few open security-related issues listed on GitHub.

To implement OpenShell, organizations need Nvidia hardware. The company's blueprint calls for Nvidia Vera Rubin infrastructure to run models like Nvidia Nemotron, with agent harnesses handled via Vera CPUs, and Nvidia BlueField-4 DPUs (aka SmartNICs) propping up Nvidia Sentry security software to monitor agent behavior.

The AI biz has made this blueprint available to partners capable of powering Linux and Kubernetes infrastructure. The usual suspects are aboard: Canonical, SUSE and Red Hat. Cloud hyperscalers Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure have also been tapped as vendors for this vision.
And of course Nvidia's floor plan applies to agents from various model builders, including Anthropic, Cohere, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Perplexity, Reflection, and SpaceX.

Nvidia says several banks – Europe’s BBVA and Santander – are perusing the OpenShell Reference Architecture spec to see how it aligns with their security and governance requirements. And the AI biz is not too modest to let slip that SAP is integrating the OpenShell Reference Architecture with its Joule Studio runtime for safer agent operations.

It's worth noting that OpenShell collects telemetry data by default, "to improve the project," Nvidia insists. The biz allows users to opt-out, with a cautionary note: "Third-party services, model providers, inference endpoints, agents, or tools that you configure and use with OpenShell may have their own terms and privacy practices." ®
b6df17c99a32ca8c: Datacenters are taking too long to bring online to fill the demand of the AI boom. So starting in 2027, Nvidia and its partners will offer its Vera Rubin rack systems fully plumbed, wired, and ready for deployment in modular bit barns.
The containers, which Nvidia calls DSX pods, were unveiled at GTC Berlin this week and are essentially the datacenter equivalent of a trailer home.
Built by partners like HPE, Dell, Schneider Electric, and others, each DSX pod will come fully furnished with all the compute, interconnects, electrical, and plumbing a growing AI factory might need.
Just drop the pod on a prepared datacenter site, hook up power, networking, and cooling, and you'll be churning out tokens and raking in profit in no time.
Or that's Nvidia's sales pitch anyway.
Inside the 28 metric ton containers you'll find seven Vera Rubin NVL72 racks packing 504 GPUs and 252 Vera CPUs.

GPUzilla says the pods will cut datacenter deployment times from six months to as little as two weeks because it will validate every fitting, cable, and component before it leaves the factory. The idea being if there is something wrong, it'll get caught there rather than after customers have gone through the trouble of hooking everything up.

And just like a trailer home, Nvidia's DSX pods will be entirely customizable. Prefer HPE over Dell, or Eaton over Schneider? No problem, Nvidia has roped all its buddies into building these compute containers.
And if you ever need more compute, just add another trailer and you've got yourself a double wide, which will surely be the envy of all your neocloud neighbors.

The first DSX pods powered by Nvidia's Vera Rubin rack systems should roll off the production line early next year, and reflect the company's ongoing effort to quash supply chain challenges before they start eating into revenues.

Also at GTC Berlin, Nvidia laid out out new DSX specs for waterless datacenters, which use closed loop coolants and dry coolers rather than water-thirsty cooling towers. This effort builds on work announced at the AI Infra Summit earlier this year, when Nvidia touted its effeorts to squeeze more performance out of less juice, while also allowing bit barns to spin down their workloads in response to changing grid conditions. ®
e988ef2e0dc7cb07: SUNGAI BULOH, Oct 21 — Three civil servants were among 27 men detained in a raid on a premises believed to be involved in the sale and processing of ketum leaves and water here today.

National Anti-Drug Agency (AADK) deputy director-general (Operations) Zainudin Abdullah said that all the individuals, aged between 19 and 61, were detained in an operation that began at 6am before being taken to the Petaling District AADK Office for documentation.
He said the premises operated daily from noon to midnight and received between 30 and 50 customers a day.
“The value of ketum sold in that location was estimated to be between RM1,000 and RM1,500 per day, with ketum water sold in a small plastic pack for RM10 and in a 1.5-litre bottle for RM20.

“Raw ketum leaves were sold at a price of between RM20 and RM40 per kilogramme (kg), while the raw material was obtained from Kedah at a price of RM12 per kg,” he said to reporters after the raid on the premises today.
Commenting further, Zainudin said the premises also offered cough syrup based on customer requests, which is believed to be used for mixing with ketum water.
He said the seized materials, including ketum leaves and ketum water, will be handed over for further investigation in collaboration with the Sungai Buloh district police headquarters (IPD).
Zainudin said that the operation was part of the Selangor-level Op Perdana, which was conducted simultaneously in six districts in the state from Monday until today to combat the activity.

He said the AADK investigation found that individual involvement in ketum abuse is increasing but following the amendment of the Drug Dependants (Treatment and Rehabilitation) Act 1983, which came into effect in August 2025, the agency is now able to take action against the abuse of the substance.

Meanwhile, an inspection of the premises located on a plot of land near the river found three large pots, each capable of boiling about 20 kg of ketum leaves at a time, while the unboiled ketum leaves were stored in an air-conditioned room to prevent them from wilting.

The premises is also equipped with closed-circuit television (CCTV), in addition to having a small window and a doorbell next to the front door, which are believed to be used for buying and selling transactions. Price tags, phone numbers, and QR codes are also displayed on the wall next to the window. — Bernama
9d2040eefdc9f9c4: JAKARTA, Oct 21 — Indonesia’s president railed today against “countries that like to insult” his nation over wildfires that have razed vast areas, spewing toxic haze into neighbouring countries.

The South-east Asian giant has for months struggled to contain fires that Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitor analysing satellite data, said have consumed more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September.

The haze has sent air pollution levels surging to dangerous levels not only at home, but also in Malaysia, Singapore and East Timor, prompting the Asean regional bloc to call a meeting over the crisis.

“As for certain countries that like to insult the Indonesian nation, when the time comes, we will reveal the companies involved” Prabowo told a cabinet meeting today, claiming that “many corporations bear responsibility” for the crisis.
He did not name names or nationalities.
The leaders of Indonesia’s neighbours have offered help while steering clear of overt criticism at the highest diplomatic level.
With public anger growing, however, a Malaysian MP last week called for Indonesia to be treated as an “outcast” in the region.
“Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” Prabowo said.
The president said he had asked for investigations into the cause of the fires which he insisted was “not purely natural”.
Experts say Indonesia’s wildfires can be blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that result in the destruction of fire-resistant forest cover and drained peatlands.
This year, the blazes were intensified by a severe drought fuelled by the El Nino weather phenomenon.
“I am asking the police, the Attorney General’s Office, the Ministry of Forestry, with the support of the Armed Forces and intelligence services, to investigate,” said Prabowo.
“The people have also caught various individuals who deliberately set fires — this is something we can regard as environmental terrorism.”

The president, who marked two years in office Tuesday with record-low approval levels, said deliberate fire-setting amounted to “a crime against humanity, because what they have done endangers the health of millions of our citizens”.
Once the evidence is in, he added, “we will revoke all licenses of companies that violate the law”. — AFP
45486bf1257f9d05: Carrie White, the telekinetic prom queen from hell, is one of the most beloved horror icons in popular culture. 3e981978a44f98dd: JAKARTA, Oct 21 — Malaysia has proposed establishing a cross-ministerial High-Level Committee (HLC) with Indonesia to accelerate bilateral cooperation in the creative industries and creative economy.

Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said that the committee would facilitate discussions on collaborative initiatives, including those that could be formalised through memoranda of understanding (MoUs) with relevant Indonesian ministries.

He said that the proposed mechanism would also help coordinate cooperation across different ministerial portfolios, as areas overseen by Malaysia’s Communications Ministry fell under several ministries in Indonesia, including those responsible for culture, communications and the creative economy.

“The intention is to expedite discussions on matters that would be covered in memoranda of understanding, which will be refined further. As I mentioned earlier, some areas fall under the purview of the Communications Ministry, while others come under several other ministries, as the portfolios are not all the same,” he said.

Fahmi spoke to Bernama after a bilateral meeting with Indonesian Creative Economy Minister Teuku Riefky Harsya here on Wednesday, during which both ministers witnessed the signing of two MoUs between Malaysia's MyCreative Ventures and two Indonesian entities, the Jakarta Creative Economy Committee and EnMasse.

Fahmi said the agreements were expected to facilitate closer collaboration and the exchange of creative industry activities between the two countries, particularly in music and related sectors.

On his meeting with Teuku Riefky, Fahmi said he was briefed on the roles and responsibilities of Indonesia’s newly established Creative Economy Ministry under President Prabowo Subianto’s administration, and that they had explored potential areas of cooperation.

“This will certainly help us examine and assess policy aspects and the implementation of programmes for the creative economy,” he said.

Earlier, Fahmi, who is on a working visit to Jakarta until Thursday, held a separate bilateral meeting with Indonesian Culture Minister Fadli Zon, following discussions with Indonesian Communication and Digital Affairs Minister Meutya Hafid on Tuesday.
Fahmi said his discussions with Fadli focused on strengthening bilateral cooperation, particularly in the film industry.

“We discussed how we could strengthen cooperation, including through an MoU, particularly in the film sector, which we see as having the potential for greater collaboration, including the development of a Nusantara film festival,” he said.
Fahmi said Fadli had also proposed closer cooperation with Malaysia to seek international recognition for Malay cultural heritage, including Jawi script.

Fahmi said the proposal could follow the example of the kebaya, which was inscribed on Unesco’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in December 2024 following a joint nomination by Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei Darussalam, Singapore and Thailand. — Bernama
51ca13b68605e7eb: The European Commission has opened an investigation under the Digital Services Act into whether Booking.com is doing enough to stop fraudsters running scams, phishing and smishing on its platform.
Officials told The Register the probe, which opened Wednesday, covers a very large online platform (one with more than 45 million EU users) and has three strands.

The first is whether Booking.com is failing to prevent fraudulent and non-compliant listings. "This is very much about people portraying themselves as the owner of premises and putting it up for rent while they are not the real owner," an EC spokesperson said.

The second is whether it does enough to counter phishing and smishing (SMS phishing), and social engineering. "Scammers take over the account of a property owner and… portray themselves as the property owner, but also take over the contact details," she said. "So they start sending messages that people need to pay additional amounts."
The Commission also suspects Booking.com is not sufficiently protecting the data of its consumers and business users.

The third strand is advertising transparency: whether the platform clearly distinguishes ads from organic results, and whether it is clear about boosted listings, where property owners pay for higher ranking.
Officials cited Booking.com's own admission in June 2024 of a 500-900 percent jump in travel scams over the previous 18 months. "What made us concerned is the very high figures," an official said.

In the Netherlands alone, more than 1,000 fraud notifications were made in the first part of 2026, causing damage of €82,000, a tenfold increase on the previous year. “This is a real problem, and this is only the Dutch element,” the official said. “We have reports like that almost from all member states… So, we have clear elements where we find that the risk assessment was not sufficient, and as you know, the risk assessment is a key tool for us.”

The Commission acknowledges that Booking.com assesses fraud using cases on its own platform and external reports, and takes internal measures in response. But “we feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” the official said. “Although they take measures, they could go much further, and they could have much more solid systems to prevent fraud.”

“In the future we expect Booking.com to do a more diligent risk assessment,” she added. That could include addressing abuse of the reservation system, rapidly removing listings when fraud is reported, checking licenses, and changing how property owners are onboarded.
A spokesperson at Booking.com told The Register:

"We are cooperating fully with the European Commission and engaging constructively on its questions under the Digital Services Act (DSA). Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com. We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect travelers and partners." ®

8f80367721f31f45: KANGAR, Oct 21 — A total of 251 passengers aboard the Express Bahagia 98 (EB98) ferry from Langkawi, which ran aground on a sandbank near the entrance to the Kuala Perlis Passenger Ferry Terminal this morning, were safely evacuated at 2.50 pm today.

Norhafiz said the EB98 ferry departed Langkawi at 9.30am before running aground at about 10.35am near Buoy No 1 in Kuala Perlis, when the captain took evasive action to avoid a fishing net stretched across the inbound and outbound shipping channel at Kuala Perlis.

3bb647f11484a118: BRUSSELS, Oct 21 — The European Union opened an investigation into online travel agent Booking.com today over alleged failures to tackle fake listings and phishing scams.
The EU fears Booking.com has underestimated the impact of fraud and unlicensed accommodation, and is not sufficiently protecting users’ data from being misused for scams.
The probe is the first into Booking.com under the Digital Services Act (DSA), a mammoth online content law that covers a wide array of platforms including social media and digital marketplaces.
“Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed,” EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said in a statement.

The EU said it was also looking into whether the Netherlands-based firm breached rules “because it did not clearly label as ads those listings whose providers paid for a higher ranking in search results shown to users”.
The DSA “sets clear responsibilities” and “we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously”, Virkkunen added.
Booking.com said that it was “cooperating fully” and that “security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities”.
“We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to combat cybercrime and online fraud and protect travellers and partners,” it added.

Booking.com is among over 20 very large online platforms that must comply with the DSA’s stricter rules or risk fines that could go as high as six per cent of their global turnover, or even a ban for serious and repeated breaches.
There is no legal deadline for the completion of the probe but the targeted company can offer commitments to address the European Commission’s concerns.
Suspicions over data
A senior EU official was critical of Booking.com and its risk assessment efforts since 2023.
“We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” the official said on condition of anonymity.

The commission — the EU’s digital watchdog — said it would assess whether the online platform “properly identified” risks linked to the spread of illegal content such as non-existent properties and fraudsters portraying themselves as the owner of a property and putting it up for rent.
In some cases, customers discover on arrival that the property they thought they had booked does not exist, or more often, photographs or property descriptions do not accurately reflect reality.
The EU will also investigate whether Booking.com is doing enough to address the risks that phishing scams pose to European consumers.
Phishing is broadly defined as the practice of tricking people into sharing sensitive information through deceptive messages.

The EU said it would look at how reservation and guest data is shared with accommodation providers, and whether Booking.com has put in place “sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused”.
“We suspect that Booking is not sufficiently protecting the data of... private users and business users, and (this) makes the system vulnerable for this kind of phishing,” the senior official said.
Meta is also under investigation over potentially fraudulent advertising on its platforms in a probe that began in 2024. — AFP
a14b3866a853e94b: Java has elbowed its way onto a Tyne and Wear Metro information display, giving passengers an error message alongside their train times.

Eagle-eyed Register reader abend0c4 spotted the sign, whose dialog design suggests a rather elderly Windows installation. Could it be Windows 7 in Classic guise, or perhaps Windows Server 2008 R2? Both wheezed their last in 2023, when the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program ended. Or perhaps POSReady 7? That kept going (again via ESU) until October 8, 2024.
Not that the end of ESU means the code will suddenly stop working. Just that Microsoft has called a halt to updates.

The Tyne and Wear Metro is no stranger to keeping old technology running past its expiration date. Opened in August 1980, the transit network has been replacing its aging rolling stock with new units, but the signage has endured. Then again, compared to the Commodore VIC-20 and Apple II, which ruled the home computing roost in 1980, perhaps an operating system that's only been obsolete for a few years isn't such a bad thing.
Any second now somebody will be writing an email about some hardware by Sinclair, Acorn, or their particular device maker of choice.
But back to the sign. Sadly, it's unclear which version of Java has elbowed its way to the foreground. Java's troubleshooting guidance lists video driver problems as one possible cause of this error.
The train indicator seems to be operating as normal if somewhat obscured by Java's attempt to be the centre of attention," our reader noted.
Java is longer be a bright young thing, yet it still keeps plenty of enterprise systems running behind the scenes. On this occasion, it appears to prefer the foreground.
We'd prefer it kept a lower profile. Passengers have enough ups and downs without Java throwing its toys out of the virtual pram. ®

17017ff06279bb45: Software developers will need to get their kicks from becoming code coaches of AI, professors of prompt engineering, and masters of their domain.

So says Pratik Wadher, chief technology officer at Kaseya, who oversaw a team of codesmiths rewriting software across the company’s managed services portfolio, which spans remote monitoring and management, backup and recovery, cybersecurity, and automation.

“The goal is unifying our data, unifying our API, but as we are starting to also look at the product portfolio that we have, we're trying to understand what are the patterns that we can use to consolidate the product workflows,” he tells The Register.

Storage is a good example. The basic workflows involve reading and writing data to storage arrays, Kaseya's own cloud environment, or the racks run by hyperscalers. The team re-architected the back end of its storage products so the storage engine reads and writes to any kind of storage from ZFS to S3.
“This is where AI helps,” Wadher claims. “Fundamentally we have accelerated that piece of re-architecture.”
Since joining Kaseya in September 2025, the CTO has been trying to simplify what he admits can be a “confusing” number of individual products.

“The storage layer that we've been writing, we re-architected and wrote it in six weeks. And that's the actual writing, implementing and testing the code. There are years of domain expertise behind understanding how we want to write it.”

In the process, Kaseya used Anthropic coding agents to help a human write the spec. The meatbags at Kaseya then iterated on it and peer-reviewed it with critique agents, before the AI generated the code. Anthropic’s Claude is becoming the “de facto standard” for writing code at Kaseya.

“When I look at my engineers, it's not how I used to write code. It's almost like I'm manipulating these agents, but the best engineers are still critical, because you have developed a lot of experience in understanding what you need to do,” Wadher says.
Does this take the fun out of coding? Yes and no, he claims. Mirroring the wider industry, some Kaseya engineers are embracing the new approach and some are more “hesitant.”

“The fun part of coding is going to be the design, the architecture, the thinking. Writing code is fun but I don't think it's [the] fun [part]. The fun part is having the code run, seeing what it can do, and then tweaking it and changing it. If you can accelerate that and start seeing the results, I think that, for me at least, that would be the fun part: seeing the impact.”

Developers must become proficient prompters and “you need the domain expertise,” he adds. “If you’re just using AI to generate code I don’t think you’re going to be useful and I don't think the code you're writing is going to be useful.”

Some Reg readers and some of the article-writing vultures may disagree. There is a clear split happening in the world of FOSS, for example, where some projects want only human-written code and others take what they describe as a more pragmatic view of AI tools.
AI is already forcing change upon the tech sector. Research last year suggested the number of graduates starting a career in technology is plunging with certain functions being subsumed by agents.
“I think basic tasks will be done by AI, so you're not going to need that,” Wadher says. “The skills that will be extremely important are critical thinking and writing.

“The worst part of coding, [the thing] engineers hate is writing the documentation. Well, guess what? That is going to become even more critical now. Being able to write clear, concise design specifications, the functional specifications, is going to be extremely important. The good thing is that you’ll now have an [AI] partner that can do this with you and you can iterate with this partner.

“I would say the new code is the spec. That's what you're going to check into GitHub now, because you want to make sure that the spec you wrote is going to generate the same type of code now over and over again. I have seen variances." ®
fe9f731859aae0c0: Mass unemployment, boiling the planet, and human extinction within a decade: the dystopian visions of AI are well rehearsed. Academics now argue that EU policymakers should ensure the taxpayers helping to fund the tech get something back, a “happiness dividend.”

Researchers at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII), led by Professor Sandra Wachter, say citizens who are inadvertently helping to create the next generation of tech billionaires need more than promises that AI will boost economic growth and fatten corporate profits.

Their paper, "Optimising for happiness in EU technology policy to repay public subsidies for AI," published in the Royal Society Open Science, notes that the public backs AI development through funding, tax breaks, and access to land, water, energy, infrastructure, and data.
On data, most people have no say in the matter. Creative work, social media posts, and user interactions have all been swept up to train frontier models, spurring a stream of lawsuits.

The OII team proposes happiness as a third goal for AI heavyweights, alongside economic growth and risk mitigation. “Making technology less harmful is not the same as making it socially beneficial,” the researchers told us.

What makes people happy? The researchers point to relatedness, competence, and autonomy, all of which some uses of AI could undermine. Chatbots that mimic human emotion may erode the value people place on real human connection. Heavy reliance on AI could dull skills. AI influence could make it harder for people to make their own choices. And datacenters threaten land and water, leaving fewer trees and green spaces for people to connect with nature.

“Under the proposed approach, companies benefiting from public support would be expected to predict how their technologies will improve happiness and well-being, and be held accountable for delivering those benefits,” the researchers said.

The EU has allocated €20 billion for AI gigafactories, while GenAI4EU and the Digital Europe programme is using €700 million through Horizon research projects into generative AI and supercomputing initiatives.

“The public already pays for AI through subsidies, resources, and data, yet has little say over what it gets in return,” said lead author Professor Sandra Wachter. “We believe people deserve technology that increases their happiness. If the public is helping to build the AI industry, it should also share in its benefits.”

Denser, more powerful servers in a growing number of datacenters are drawing more energy, potentially pushing up household electricity bills. Memory makers are prioritizing higher-margin chips, so ordinary DRAM and NAND cost more, and so do the devices that use them. Water, which some see as the planet’s next most precious commodity, is being used to cool server racks.

Anthropic warned this year that humanity risks courting extinction unless powerful models are properly controlled. Last year it and OpenAI raised the prospect of mass unemployment as employers turn to AI to cut costs. The researchers add that the difficulty of getting data out of model makers and their cloud providers makes it harder to gauge the environmental damage datacenters are doing.

Against that backdrop, finding some way to improve people’s well-being looks essential. Will the model makers take note? Even pessimists are sometimes pleasantly surprised, though we expect profits will trump pleasantness. ®

5b3ce3d240be4172: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”

I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)

My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near ­constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine.

If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now.
We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious.

Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing. That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular.

We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with.

It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible.

Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.
So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.
I hope you enjoy the ride.
2ee0182f23a97c23: Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-­powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.

Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.”

Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going. The US has started—and terminated—several programs looking into it over the past 75 years. The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which ended in 2025. The project was canceled because of high experimentation costs, an inability to compete with conventional rocket propulsion on price, and difficulty ensuring that ground tests could be performed safely and effectively. (You are creating an incredibly powerful nuclear reaction, after all.)

After much wavering, it now appears that nuclear-powered interplanetary travel is a $2 billion bet NASA is willing to make. The agency is pursuing an approach called nuclear electric propulsion, which uses the neutrons produced in a self-­sustaining, uranium-­atom-splitting reaction to create heat and ultimately electricity. The electricity is used to ionize a gas, which is blasted out of the spacecraft with the help of magnetic fields, generating thrust. The approach “is very low thrust, but very efficient,” says Sebastian Corbisiero, the US Department of Energy’s national technical director of space reactor programs. “So you can use it for a long period of time.”

What might such a rocket look like? A presentation by Steve Sinacore, program director of NASA’s SR-1 program, offers some clues. So far, the concept art makes the craft look like a colossal fletched arrow. The back will house the power-and-propulsion system, while the tip will hold a uranium-filled nuclear reactor with a capacity of at least 20 kilowatts. (For context, a typical nuclear plant on Earth is about 50,000 times more powerful.) The “fletches” on SR-1 are large fins that help cool the reactor by radiating heat into space.

Like many other pieces of space hardware, the reactor will need to be put through its paces on the ground before it’s cleared for the rough rocket trip to space. “Going through the launch safely is going to be a challenge,” says Middleburgh. “You are being shaken, rattled, and rolled.” For safety reasons, the reactor will be switched on around two days post-launch, when it’s comfortably far from Earth. Uranium isn’t tremendously dangerous by itself, but that can’t be said of the waste products that emerge when the reactor is running. If SR-1 works as planned, its journey to Mars will take about a year.

Will this novel form of space propulsion actually reach the Red Planet by 2029? It’s possible. NASA says the Idaho National Laboratory, which is building SR-1’s reactor, is making progress and is on target for a late-2028 launch. “Procurement of major components is underway, and integration work on the power and propulsion element is advancing steadily,” Sinacore told MIT Technology Review. The outlook will get even sunnier if the Artemis program, which aims to start laying the foundations for a base on the lunar south pole by the decade’s end, keeps to its own bold deadline.

“It’s an aggressive timeline,” says Lindsey Holmes, who is vice president of advanced projects at Analytical Mechanics Associates, an aerospace company in Virginia. She suspects the push is being driven partly by China’s and Russia’s own deep-space nuclear ambitions. The two countries have spoken about plans to place a reactor on the moon’s surface in the mid-2030s to power a jointly operated lunar base. Whether it flies or fails in space, SR-1’s development should help NASA put its own reactor on the moon; the technology involved in the two projects is broadly similar, given that the lunar surface, like space itself, is a vacuum. If an interplanetary nuclear-powered spacecraft works, a nuclear reactor on the moon should too.
Most of the technology for SR-1 already exists; it’s going to come down to piecing it all together and then seeing how it performs in space.
a25affc9ec1890c4: We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.

It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health. But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step. Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs. That’s a tall order: More than 90% of treatments that enter human studies fail.

There are regulatory hurdles too. The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia.

There may never be a pill that delivers all the benefits of exercise, but research could lead to new medicines that mimic some aspects of working out. Scientists have already identified many important exercise-related signals and have even developed compounds to regulate them. (Some preliminary results have been so promising that doping authorities have proactively banned the compounds.)

Burris and his colleagues are focused on a receptor that’s always switched on, even without exercise. Working out appears to boost that receptor in muscle cells, which in turn helps bolster endurance over time. Burris’s lab has spent years designing a drug that cranks up the receptor’s activity directly, and mice treated with the drug ran longer and farther than mice that weren’t. They “become marathon mice without having to do any type of exercise,” Burris says. There are even indications—also in mice—that the compound mimics some of the cognitive benefits of exercise and could help treat heart failure. Burris founded a company called Pelagos to carry the work forward into a clinical trial.

Other workout-mimicking drugs have already entered human studies. In June, the biotech firm Cambrian Bio reported that its experimental drug ATX-304 boosted metabolism and reduced liver and belly fat in people with obesity and prediabetes. It activates a metabolic switch that helps cells sense when energy supplies dip and coordinates the production of more fuel—the same switch that helps us sustain long sessions jumping rope or swimming laps. Cambrian hopes it will help people lose weight without losing muscle, a common concern with GLP-1 medicines.
Our understanding of how exercise benefits the body is still coming into focus, and drug development is prone to failure.
59f0b17775a71ce5: Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech.

Teasing all this out is complex. To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them. Prairie dogs, for example, utter a different series of yips when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby. It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-­observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats.

There are other hurdles. Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive. And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate.

Over the past 50 years, a growing arsenal of devices has made it easier to observe the sophisticated ways animals communicate. Hydrophones at the bottom of the ocean can capture humpback whale song, and tiny wearable “biologgers” can record a bat’s every squeak.

In the last decade, advances in AI have leveled up our ability to make sense of it all. The technology can detect different calls, distinguish which sounds belong to which animal, and spot patterns. Researchers at the Earth Species Project (ESP), a nonprofit founded in 2018 to decode animal communication, recently used machine learning to detect vocalizations of carrion crows and determine which bird made which call.

They suspect that more advanced AI could translate critters’ chatter. Large language models like Claude and ChatGPT excel at finding relationships between words, explains Sara Keen, one of ESP’s behavioral ecologists. ESP hopes its own NatureLM—trained on human speech, music, and animal sounds—will be able to interpret the vocalizations of a variety of species.

That promise, however, is still theoretical. Yossi Yovel, a neuroecologist at Tel Aviv University, worries that these models will put too much emphasis on acoustic similarities and make mistakes—like lumping together similar sounds that have different meanings.

As for a two-way convo? It’s not clear when—or whether—that will happen. Still, “a lot of animals have an evolutionary structure that is similar enough that we should be able to understand what they’re saying,” Slobodchikoff says.
Researchers have amassed heaps of data on animal communication, but they’re still trying to figure out how to decipher it all.
d1384ab5fdd08b1f: Scrubbing Earth of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—a.k.a. PFAS or forever chemicals—could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS have been linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response. They are known for a strong bond between carbon and fluorine, which the environment struggles to break down.

PFAS are everywhere: They spew from factories and slough off products and into water with normal use. Scientists have found them in everything from human blood to Antarctic snow. One 2022 report found that 89% of the US population had PFAS in excess of two nanograms per milliliter of blood plasma, a common threshold for potential adverse health effects, and 9% of the population had passed the riskier level of 20 nanograms per milliliter.
The PFAS monster is also a moving target. New compounds are still being created and used. There are more than 12,000 of them, and much of the cleanup research focuses on only a small handful.

Cleansing PFAS-contaminated soil is a project in its infancy, but it is possible to prevent more buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems. There are two ways to handle this: trap or destroy. Some scientists have found reverse osmosis—a process that pushes water through supertight filters—useful in point-of-use cases, like water filters at kitchen sinks.

Other techniques in the pipeline might be more suitable for large-scale removal—for example, at water treatment facilities. One, called foam fractionation, generates bubbles that capture PFAS. More approaches, like ensnaring the chemicals in nanothin layers of charged metal, are also under investigation.
Trapping, though, is imperfect. You’re left with PFAS-filled brine, which if not properly destroyed (an expensive and energy-sucking endeavor) can still end up in the environment.

Jack Huang, a professor of crop and soil sciences at the University of Georgia, is working on destruction. He’s testing a method called electrochemical degradation, which uses electrodes to break down the bonds that hold PFAS together. The product destroyed more than 90% of PFAS mass in tests and has already been licensed by the engineering consulting firm AECOM.

Ridding life of PFAS is also a policy challenge. There are alternatives; we just need the push to use them. And we’ve had success before: The EPA’s 2010/2015 PFOA Stewardship Program has helped slash the release of water-repellent perfluorooctanoic acid by 95%. More recently, Minnesota, Maine, and New Mexico have passed bans on PFAS in products like cookware and dental floss.
Scientists are making strides toward removing and destroying PFAS—but it’ll be all for naught if we don’t turn off the tap.
1edb1aac3a288182: The rise of the lithium-ion battery, which powers everything from the smallest personal electronics to gargantuan energy storage systems, has been nothing short of revolutionary. But as anyone who’s boarded a plane in the last decade could tell you, storing and pumping out energy by moving charged lithium ions through a liquid electrolyte soup has its drawbacks, not least that the batteries have a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer, creating power packs that charge faster, last longer, cram more energy into smaller spaces, and (crucially) run cooler. A new generation of companies aim to bring such batteries to market, and if their bets pan out, the tech could substantially ease the shift away from fossil fuels.

Solid-state batteries have been “just a few years away” for more than a decade now. In laboratories, the technology works. But there have been challenges. In designs that pair the solid electrolyte with a lithium-metal anode (the side of the battery that releases electrons into an electrical circuit), needlelike filaments called dendrites tend to grow during charging, and they eventually push through the electrolyte and short the cell. Solid electrolytes are supposed to physically block the formation of dendrites, but many of them crack as the treelike projections break through like roots in a concrete foundation.

Then there’s the problem of manufacturing at scale. Mass production requires large quantities of defect-free sheets of ceramic-like material to make the electrolytes as well as dry rooms for assembly, since those electrolytes have a tendency to react with water. Would-be manufacturers quote a range of potential prices for solid-state batteries, but most expect them to fall in line with lithium-ion packs sometime in the mid-2030s.

Nascent as the technology is, solid-state batteries have already seen high-­profile missteps. But one of America’s most advanced solid-state-battery companies says it’s closing in on being able to bring its product to market. The Bill Gates–backed QuantumScape launched in Silicon Valley in 2010 and built its battery around a class of ceramic materials that it says is compatible with lithium—meaning no dendrite formation. “We spent, then, like 10 years learning how to process it to satisfy all of the other requirements,” says Tim Holme, QuantumScape’s cofounder and chief technology officer. In 2025, the startup announced a proprietary, large-scale manufacturing method for quickly producing and heat-treating the ceramic electrolytes used in its batteries. “Nobody has ever done this in the field of ceramics before,” Holme claims. For 10,000 years, producing ceramics has involved slowly cooking the starting materials in an oven over the course of days. “We figured out a way to shorten that down to several minutes,” he says.

Plenty of other companies are pushing the tech forward as well. Toyota, the world’s biggest automaker, launched a research program on solid-state batteries way back in 2010. It’s now partnering with the global energy and petroleum company Idemitsu Kosan on a pilot plant, promising cars that can travel up to 745 miles after charging 10 minutes or less—a huge leap, if it works out. In China, CATL, the giant behind roughly 40% of the global battery market, is aggressively pursuing solid-state batteries too, pumping nearly $2.6 billion into a research program in 2024 alone. Mercedes, meanwhile, equipped one of its EQS sedans with solid-state batteries last fall; after driving nonstop for 750 miles, the car still had some range to spare.

Will the tech gain traction? Investing in vehicle batteries makes sense given the size of the potential market. But any little uptick in cost typically gets passed on to buyers, so the first solid-state EV batteries will inevitably be more expensive.

Grid storage buyers, who are working to meet the increasing demands posed by data centers, may also hesitate to purchase new technologies that still haven’t come down the cost curve. Then again, the promise of energy storage that lasts longer than lithium-­ion’s typical eight hours could make them easier to persuade.

Some companies are taking a page from a playbook employed by outfits pursuing fusion: Focus on near-term markets with better margins to help fund development and bring down costs. Solid-state firms including California-based Solid Energies and Arizona-headquartered Sion Power are looking at selling batteries to the aviation industry or the military. “Those are sectors that are less sensitive to cost, and they typically require lower volumes as well,” says Evelina Stoikou, head analyst for battery technologies and supply chains at the consultancy BloombergNEF. “It’s a good way to prove your concept, then go through and fund the pilot plant where you can make that and eventually scale up.”
The technology works, the capital is there, and demand is not far behind. But as with anything in manufacturing, unknown unknowns remain.
3cb007058ababbd5: Every year, traffic crashes kill more than one million people, and they’re the leading cause of death for children and young adults. In the US, 100 people a day lose their lives this way, in many cases not on highways but on rural and local streets. “Traffic deaths are a leading cause of preventable death, yet we treat it like it’s inevitable,” says Leah Shahum, founder and director of the Vision Zero Network, a nonprofit focused on making streets less deadly.

The causes of a crash can be muddy. Drivers make mistakes like speeding or getting distracted, but infrastructure fails them too: Perhaps they were on a road built for speed and not safety, in a screen-filled vehicle, or at an intersection where pedestrians, cyclists, and other cars aren’t visible.

Cheap and proven traffic-calming opportunities abound—from using planters to tighten intersections to lowering speed limits—but government logjams and red tape can be speed bumps. “There’s so many moving parts,” says Laura Sandt of the University of North Carolina Highway Safety Research Center. “On the flip side, it shows that we have so many opportunities for injury prevention.”

The total number of traffic deaths has increased over the last century. And though the US rate has dipped from a peak of 30.8 deaths per 100,000 people in the 1930s, the past decade has seen a concerning jump in deadly pedestrian incidents. At the same time, communities are waking up to the essential role of traffic safety policy, Shahum says.

One success story is Hoboken, New Jersey, which hasn’t had a traffic fatality since 2017. This is due to a combination of efforts like boosting investment in public transit, promoting walkability by extending curbs, and using cameras to identify crash-prone intersections in need of a redesign. But even there, obstacles remain. If an intersection hasn’t been proved to be deadly, for example, it can be an uphill battle to argue for removing parking spaces to widen curbs. “You’re kind of selling insurance through these improvements, and that’s not always easy,” says Greg Francese, the city’s acting director of transportation and parking.

There’s also no silver bullet that will work everywhere. Situated directly across the river from New York City, Hoboken is a highly transit-oriented city of less than 60,000 people. Success there might not translate to traffic-death hot spots like Memphis or Dallas. But it’s not impossible. Take Edmonton, Alberta, a sprawling, car-centric Canadian city of around one million people: Between 2015 and 2020, it cut traffic fatalities by 63% and serious injuries by 40% by adjusting speed limits and improving signals at crosswalks.
We know how to tweak intersections and adjust traffic signals. Getting the funding and will to roll out those changes is the big red light.
f9d5ab1faea0772a: Britain is funding the next generation of tech companies without making sure taxpayers get a slice of the action, MPs have warned.

In a new report shared with The Register ahead of publication, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has accused UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) of being overly cautious about protecting taxpayers' interests. Rather than simply handing out grants, MPs want UKRI to consider taking equity stakes in more of the businesses it backs, giving the public a chance to cash in when those companies succeed.

According to the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), UK universities produce more spinouts and patents per pound of research funding than their US counterparts. But Britain is less adept at cashing in on its inventions.

British startups still struggle to attract the investment needed to grow without moving overseas, while universities have a patchy record when it comes to exploiting their intellectual property. UKRI, meanwhile, has been reluctant to impose tougher conditions on the research it funds, arguing that doing so could discourage companies from growing.

“This approach is far too cautious and we urge the Department to do much more to recover taxpayer's money when a successful company exploits research which the taxpayer, via UKRI, has paid for," the PAC said. It wants UKRI to review its standard funding terms, including whether it should take equity stakes in more companies benefiting from public money.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the PAC, acknowledged that calling for the government to behave more like a venture capitalist might seem an odd position for a committee normally concerned with keeping public spending in check.

"It may strike followers of this Committee's work that our call for government to take a less cautious approach to taking a direct stake in British innovation is an unusual one," he said. "But we are a body dedicated to value for taxpayers' money, not hoarding it. The nations currently leading the global tech race did not achieve their positions by avoiding more entrepreneurial policies. This is a simple case for the government of nothing ventured, nothing gained."

The government has made some effort to help British tech firms. UKRI gives AI startups free access to taxpayer-funded supercomputers, while DSIT has changed its procurement rules to give UK companies a better shot at supplying £400 million worth of specialist AI chips.

The British Business Bank is also investing alongside pension funds, giving taxpayers a stake in some of the businesses receiving support. But efforts to attract more pension fund investment have been slower than ministers hoped, and MPs want DSIT to start measuring whether its various support schemes are actually helping British companies grow, rather than simply counting how much money it hands out.

There's also the question of where all that research funding ends up. London, the South East, and the East of England continue to receive half of UKRI's funding, despite years of government promises to spread investment more evenly across the country.

The North's share has improved from 12 to 20 percent over the past five years, but UKRI has yet to set specific regional funding targets. Clifton-Brown described the divide as "continuing and unacceptable," warning that progress could easily be reversed without a more deliberate effort to spread the cash around.
And while MPs want UKRI to be more adventurous with its investments, they're considerably less impressed with how it manages some of the projects already on its books.

The committee pointed to an airborne laboratory upgrade that UKRI abandoned after spending £46 million of its £49 million budget. Funding was finally canceled five years after the decision to upgrade the aircraft, prompting MPs to question why the plug hadn't been pulled sooner.

Elsewhere, around 45 percent of the Science and Technology Facilities Council's estate is in unacceptable condition, and restoring university-owned research infrastructure to full working order would cost an estimated £5.6 billion. The PAC also criticized UKRI for failing to ensure a replacement for the ARCHER2 national supercomputer would be ready before the existing machine shuts down, leaving an expected 13-month gap.
It seems Whitehall has mastered the art of spending money on innovation, but getting any back is another matter. ®

75d984f22bf8022b: Google has fixed the flaws in the Chromium browser engine that saw it poll DNS root servers, but ISPs who seem to have odd views about resilience now emerged as a new source of probably-well-meaning overconsumption of internet resources.

ICANN’s office of the Chief Technology Officer delivered that view on Monday during the governance org’s annual conference in Bali, Indonesia, in a session that shared recent data from its Identifier Technology Health Indicators (ITHI) research program which monitors the security, stability and resilience of the domain name system.

ICANN principal technologist Maud Durand opened with a discussion of “Chromioids” the odd flaw in Chrome that meant well-meaning efforts to avoid a form of DNS hijacking caused the browser to generate about half of all DNS root server traffic during the year 2020.
Given Chrome’s enormous prevalence, that traffic was unwelcome.

ICANN, plus other internetworking and governance stakeholders, told Google to sort it out. Durand said the Chocolate Factory gradually did. ICANN has kept measuring the impact Chrome makes and Durand shared the graph below which shows the browser’s share of DNS root server traffic falling from 45 percent to one percent today.
Or as Durand described it, “in the noise.”
ICANN has now detected a new source of odd DNS traffic: ISPs that use multiple DNS servers for every one of their customers’ requests.

“Every single DNS query is sent three times: to Google, to Cloudflare, and to another DNS resolver,” Durand said, labelling this practice a “belt and suspenders” approach because a single resolver usually suffices to keep services up.
It’s good practice to specify primary and secondary DNS resolvers, in case one doesn’t work. But DNS resolvers are already very resilient, and making multiple requests is unusual.

The ISPs ICANN has spotted send DNS requests over IPv4 and IPv6, and for non-cached requests repeat them within 100 milliseconds for about half of queries. A further 30 percent repeat within thirty seconds.

“It is hard to know if it is a bug or a specific behaviour,” Durand said, before advancing a personal theory that the ISPs who use this odd resilience technique can’t hire skilled internetworking engineers and therefore created a kind of brute-force resilience routine. The organization is researching the cause.
ICANN feels the ISPs using this practice aren’t major players, but the org worries that if the practice becomes widespread, or is adopted by a large entity, it could have a nasty impact.
Pointlessly busy DNS servers also matter because ICANN thinks the number of DNS service providers is becoming more concentrated.

ICANN has tried to calculate how many DNS resolvers half of internet users can “see” when they are online. As the graph below shows, users could see almost 250 resolver farms in the year 2020. That figure is just under 150 today.
Again, Durand isn’t sure why but suspects the number of DNS resolver operators might be shrinking and that the remaining visible resolvers belong to tech giants. ®
